breath-support.title: Breath support (appoggio)
breath-support.why: A steady, supported airstream is the engine of good singing. Without it, pitch drifts, tone wavers, and phrases collapse at the end. Support comes from managing the exhale with the breathing muscles rather than pushing from the throat.
cues: Breathe low: let the belly and lower ribs expand, keep shoulders still.
Sing on a steady, gently resisted airstream (imagine sustaining a candle flame without blowing it out).
Keep the ribs expanded through the phrase instead of collapsing immediately.

exercises.title: Hiss exercise
exercises.instruction: Inhale for 4 counts, then hiss on 's' for 12–16 seconds. Keep the stream perfectly even — no pulses, no fade at the end.

exercises.title: Supported siren
exercises.instruction: Lip-trill or 'ng' siren from low to high and back, 8–10 seconds, without the air collapsing at the top.

exercises.title: Phrase on 'oo'
exercises.instruction: Sing the phrase on a steady 'oo'. Ignore words. Only the airstream matters — unwavering from first note to last.

pitch-accuracy.title: Pitch accuracy
pitch-accuracy.why: Landing in the center of each note is a trained skill of ear plus coordination. Singing flat usually means low breath energy or a heavy larynx; singing sharp often means excess tension. Slow, deliberate matching retrains the coordination.
cues: Hear the target pitch in your mind before you sing it.
If you tend flat, lead each note with breath energy so it blooms up to center.
If you tend sharp, relax the jaw and larynx and approach the note from just under center.

exercises.title: Slow note matching
exercises.instruction: Sing the phrase at half speed. Hold each note until it is centered on the play-along pitch before moving on.

exercises.title: Siren through the range
exercises.instruction: Glide smoothly through the phrase's range on 'oo'. No jumps, no breaks — a continuous line.

exercises.title: Phrase at full tempo
exercises.instruction: Sing the melody on 'ah'. Aim for the center of each written note — a perfectly tuned wrong note still fails.

forward-resonance.title: Forward resonance (placement)
forward-resonance.why: A tone can be on pitch yet sound thin or dull if it lacks resonance. Bringing the sound 'forward' into the mask strengthens the 2nd and 3rd harmonics, which the ear reads as a ringing, present, carrying voice.
cues: Find a buzz on the lips and front of the face, not in the throat.
Keep that forward 'ping' as you open from a hum into the vowel.
Think of the sound spinning forward and up, toward the front teeth.

exercises.title: Ng to ah slides
exercises.instruction: On each note of the phrase, start on 'ng' (buzz in the mask) then open to 'ah' without losing the buzz.

exercises.title: Hum the phrase
exercises.instruction: Hum the melody with lips closed. Feel the buzz on the front teeth and nose. Keep it even.

exercises.title: Nyah placement
exercises.instruction: Sing the melody on a bratty 'nyah', then immediately again on a clean 'ah' keeping the same forward ping.

open-throat.title: Open throat (relaxed resonance space)
open-throat.why: A tight or squeezed throat chokes the tone and tires the voice. A relaxed, open pharynx (the feeling at the start of a yawn) lets the sound resonate freely and stay healthy across a phrase.
cues: Feel the gentle openness of the start of a yawn, without forcing it.
Keep the jaw loose and the tongue relaxed and forward.
Maintain the open space consistently rather than only on high notes.

exercises.title: Yawn-sigh glides
exercises.instruction: Start a silent yawn, then sigh on 'ah' from the top of your range to the bottom. Jaw stays loose.

exercises.title: Phrase on open 'ah'
exercises.instruction: Sing the phrase on 'ah' with a comfortably dropped jaw. Do not clench. Keep the yawn-space through every note.

exercises.title: Ee–ah on one pitch
exercises.instruction: Pick a comfortable mid note. Alternate 'ee' and 'ah' four times without changing the throat space.
